svg.title: An everyday change goes from an issue to a released version — An issue becomes a merge request, and main releases the change
svg.text: An everyday change goes from an issue to a released
Scenario: An issue becomes a merge request, and main releases the change
The change rides a merge request

g.text: Given an installed project with the framework already on its main
branch
A project that already ran the installer: main carries the whole framework, with its
automation tokens wired so the release can run on its own. The developer is signed in — this
is where a new day of work begins.
When the developer opens an issue for a small change
An issue is a ticket describing the work. This one asks for a short line in the README.
Opening it first is how a change starts here — and the issue page already offers the next
move: the "Create merge request" button.
And the developer creates the merge request from the issue and takes it
The merge request is created straight from the issue — GitLab names its branch after the
ticket and links the two — and the developer takes the work by assigning the merge request
to themself.
When the developer clones the project into a fresh workspace folder
The developer starts from a clean slate, the way real work starts: a workspace folder named
after the project's address, a fresh clone inside it, and the issue's branch checked out.
And the developer adds the line to the README
The change itself: one line added at the end of the README. This is the everyday edit the
whole story is about.

text.tspan: echo "This project was scaffolded with The DevSecOps Toolbox." >> README.md

g.text: And the developer commits the change as a conventional feat
The commit message follows Conventional Commits (feat: a new feature) — the release tooling
reads it later to pick the next version. The card shows the commit command and git's own
answer.

text.tspan: git commit -m "feat: mention the toolbox in the readme"

g.text: And the developer pushes the branch to GitLab
Pushing the branch updates the merge request and starts its pipeline (the automatic checks
that must pass before the change can merge).
Then the merge request's pipeline turns green
The full inherited pipeline runs on the change and every job passes: the merge request now
says so, and the merge button is unlocked. Main only accepts a change once these checks are
green.
When the reviewed change merges into main
With the pipeline green, the merge request is merged. The branch joins main through review,
never a forced push, and the issue closes itself.
Then the project home now shows the change on main
The project's home page right after the merge: the feat commit sits on top of main and the
README now ends with the developer's line.
And main's own pipeline runs the release
The merge started main's own pipeline, with the release stage in it — no one asked for a
release, the pipeline just includes it. It ran green from start to finish.
And the release job's own log confirms the version move
Inside the release job's log: Commitizen reads the feat commit, moves the version from 0.1.0
to 0.2.0 and stamps the tag. These are the job's own lines.
And GitLab's tags page now shows 0.2.0
The tags page now shows 0.2.0 — plain, with no v in front — carrying the release commit.
And the project files on main now carry the release
The release is also visible in the files: main's tree now opens on the bump commit, with the
README carrying the developer's line.
And VERSION and the version config really moved to 0.2.0
The proof in the files themselves: VERSION reads 0.2.0, and the release commit touched
exactly the two files that track the version — VERSION and the Commitizen config inside
.config.
And the developer removes the local clone, ready to start clean next
time
Work done, the developer deletes the local clone. Nothing is lost — GitLab holds the branch,
the merge, the tag — and the next change will start from a fresh clone, exactly like this
one did.
